result: The authors generated a new collection of over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA driver lines covering approximately 300 cell types, including sensory neurons, projection neurons, interneurons, and other cell types relevant to mushroom body circuits. The collection was created by screening over 4000 intersections, selecting 1183 lines for further characterization, and ultimately identifying 828 experimentally useful lines based on specificity, intensity, and consistency. These lines are publicly available with 28,376 confocal images from 6374 tissue samples.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core contribution. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'successfully generated over 800 split-GAL4 drivers and 22 split-LexA drivers covering a substantial number of neuron types.' Reviewers 2 and 3 similarly acknowledge the collection as 'comprehensive' and 'vastly extends the number of driver lines available.' The methodology and scale are accepted without critique.

result: The split-GAL4 lines were annotated by matching labeled neurons to their counterparts in the hemibrain connectome volume using confocal images registered to a standard brain. This light microscopy to EM matching process enables users to select driver lines based on upstream and downstream synaptic partners in the connectome map.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise this aspect. Reviewer 3 notes 'Driver expression patterns are beautifully illustrated side-by-side with corresponding skeletonized neurons reconstructed by EM' and that 'the authors have identified the targeted cell types within the Drosophila connectome.' Reviewer 1 confirms the authors 'correlated them with identified neuron types from the Hemibrain EM connectome by matching light microscopy images to neuronal shapes defined by EM.' No concerns are raised about this methodology.

result: The collection includes split-GAL4 drivers for 110 cell types that connect with DANs and MBONs, covering 30 types of 'major interneurons' (those with over 100 total synaptic inputs from MBONs and/or outputs to DANs). Specific examples include CRE011, which integrates over 2000 inputs from nine types of MBONs (the highest among all interneurons) and provides cholinergic input to reward DANs, and SMP108, which receives inputs from multiple glutamatergic MBONs and makes the highest number of cholinergic connections to DANs involved in appetitive memory.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly highlights this contribution: 'The characterization of split-GAL4 drivers for 30 major interneurons connected with DANs and/or MBONs in this study will significantly contribute to our understanding of recurrent connections in mushroom body function.' The specific examples and connectivity data are presented without challenge from any reviewer.

result: The authors developed 191 driver lines for projection neurons (PNs) and other cell types in the antennal lobe, covering more than 48 of the approximately 190 PN types identified through EM connectome and LM studies. This includes both uni- and multi-glomerular PNs, as well as 8 lines for sensory neurons and 18 lines for projection neurons associated with the 7 non-olfactory glomeruli involved in thermo- and hygro-sensory processing.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the breadth of the collection without raising concerns about the PN drivers. The comprehensive nature of the resource is consistently praised across all reviews, implicitly supporting the inclusion of these sensory input pathways.

result: The authors refined Gr64f-GAL4 expression by generating 16 stable split-GAL4 lines with labeling in distinct subsets of gustatory sensory neurons. SS87269 emerged as the best driver for substituting sugar reward in olfactory learning, expressing in labellum and tarsal sensory neurons (atGRN and stGRN types) but lacking expression in pharyngeal, abdominal ganglion, and olfactory sensory neurons. Activation of SS87269 neurons produced robust appetitive memories, proboscis extension, slowed locomotion, and strong local search behavior that was superior to other Gr64f-split-GAL4 drivers and the original Gr64f-GAL4.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically praises this work: 'the authors have elaborated on a series of intersectional drivers with GR64f-GAL4 to dissect subsets of labeled neurons. This approach successfully identified a more specific sugar sensory neuron driver, SS87269, which consistently exhibited optimal training performance and triggered ethologically relevant local searching behaviors. This newly characterized line could serve as an optimized optogenetic tool for sugar reward in future studies.' Reviewer 2 also notes this as 'functionally validated.' The behavioral data supporting SS87269's superiority is accepted without critique.

result: Two other Gr64f-split-GAL4 lines (SS87278 and SS87279) express in cells that appear to convey aversive signals. Activation of these lines induced increased walking speed, reduced probability of revisiting activation sites, and progressively reduced mobility during inter-trial intervals. With extended training, preference to the paired odor became negative. These drivers label distinct subsets of sensory neurons projecting to the abdominal ganglion, with SS87278 showing innervation similar to Gr66a-GAL4 and projecting to the abdominal body surface, likely representing class IV multidendritic neurons that detect multimodal nociceptive stimuli.
evaluation: While reviewers do not explicitly discuss these aversive lines, the overall functional characterization of the Gr64f refinement is praised by Reviewer 1, and the comprehensive behavioral testing is acknowledged. The anatomical identification of these neurons as nociceptive is consistent with the cited literature and not challenged.

result: The authors generated driver lines for putative ascending nociceptive pathways. Through optogenetic testing of 581 hemidriver combinations in a quadrant avoidance assay, they identified SS01159 as showing the most robust avoidance of illuminated quadrants with behavioral features characteristic of nociception (backward walking, turning, increased speed, and jumping). This driver labels a group of ascending neurons that likely carry nociceptive signals from the body and legs to the brain.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the collection includes 'putative nociceptive ascending neurons' (Reviewer 1) and that 'a driver for putative nociceptive ascending neurons, potentially serving as optogenetic negative reinforcement, is characterized by optogenetic avoidance behavior.' The functional validation through behavioral testing is accepted without critique.

result: While annotating over 6000 confocal images, the authors occasionally encountered samples with atypical morphologies. Examples include a V_l2PN neuron projecting to the contralateral hemisphere, a brain with two DPM neurons in one hemisphere with atypical calyx innervation, MBON-α1 with projections to the ellipsoid body, and MBON-α3 with variable soma positions. Overall, in 1241 brain hemispheres examined, mislocalization of dendrites and axons was found in 3.14% and 0.97% of MB cell types, respectively. These rare variations are considered erroneous projections from stochastic developmental processes or possibly ectopic reporter expression.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges this finding: 'The authors also use their very large dataset of neuronal anatomies, covering many example neurons from many brains, to identify neuron instances with atypical morphology. They find many examples of mushroom body neurons with altered neuronal numbers or mistargeting of dendrites or axons and estimate that 1-3% of neurons in each brain may have anatomic peculiarities or malformations.' Reviewer 2 notes these 'discoveries might open new avenues for future investigations into how such asymmetry and individuality arise.'

result: The authors observed frequent and reproducible variations in MBON08 and MBON09 labeled by MB083C. The driver invariably labels two cells per hemisphere in 169 brain samples, with dendrites in γ3 and β'2a compartments. MCFO revealed two distinct morphologies: MBON08 arborizes in γ3 of both hemispheres, while MBON09 arborizes in ipsilateral γ3 and contralateral β'2a. β'2a was always labeled in both hemispheres, suggesting MBON09 is always present. In MCFO experiments, 21 instances of MBON08 and 188 instances of MBON09 were observed. Based on these observations, 65% of flies are expected to contain four MBON09, while 35% likely have at least one MBON08. MBON08 was never observed in both hemispheres or twice in one hemisphere. This asymmetry could be a source of turning handedness and idiosyncratic learning performance.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 provides strong support: 'Significantly, the study systematically assesses the individualized existence of MBON08 for the first time. This neuron is a variant shape that sometimes occurs instead of one of two copies of MBON09, and this variation is more common than that in other neuronal classes: 75% of hemispheres have two MBON09's, and 25% have one MBON09 and one MBON08... This remarkable phenotype potentially serves as a valuable resource for understanding the stochasticity of neurodevelopment.' Reviewer 2 notes this as an example of 'asymmetry and individuality' that 'might open new avenues for future investigations.'

result: To broaden the utility of frequently used split-GAL4 lines, the authors generated over 20 LexADBD lines to test conversions of split-GAL4 to split-LexA. The majority (22 out of 34) of resulting split-LexA lines exhibited very similar expression patterns to their corresponding original split-GAL4 lines. The main mode of failure was that expression levels became too weak and stochastic.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the collection includes split-LexA drivers (Reviewer 1 mentions '22 split-LexA drivers'). The conversion success rate and failure mode are presented as technical observations without challenge from reviewers.
